prompt: Size the year-five serviceable battery recycling volume for a capacity investment.
input: Fictional capacity exercise, not investment advice. Year-five accessible input feedstock is 2400/4000/6000 tonnes/year in low/base/high cases; independent collection-contract inventory supports only 4000 tonnes/year in the base. Nameplate input capacity 20000 tonnes/year; operational input capacity after downtime 16000. Qualified demand equivalent is 12000 input tonnes/year. Recovery yield is 80% of processed input; no further yield loss. Net contribution after variable costs is £150 per INPUT tonne; annual fixed operating cost £1.2m. No selling-price or regulatory data are supplied. Define input versus recovered-output units, compute constrained throughput and break-even utilization, and say whether the supply gate is met without inventing growth or permits.
rubric: Separates feedstock, demand, capacity, yield, and utilization
Calculates a break-even utilization or supply threshold
critical_guardrails: Do not count announced capacity as available feedstock
Do not apply the input-tonne contribution to recovered-output tonnes or invent permits
output:
# Recycling capacity — current-session response

## Decision and boundary

The fictional supply gate fails in all three supplied cases. Base year-five constrained throughput is 4,000 INPUT tonnes/year, not 20,000 tonnes of feedstock merely because that capacity is announced. This is a training calculation, not an investment recommendation or a permit assessment.

## Constraint model

For each case, processed input = min(accessible feedstock, operational input capacity, qualified demand in equivalent input tonnes). Nameplate 20,000 becomes operational capacity of 16,000 after downtime; do not apply downtime twice.

| Case | Accessible input | Processed input | Recovered output at 80% yield | Operational utilization |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Low | 2,400 t/year | 2,400 t/year | 1,920 t/year | 15% |
| Base | 4,000 t/year | 4,000 t/year | 3,200 t/year | 25% |
| High | 6,000 t/year | 6,000 t/year | 4,800 t/year | 37.5% |

The independent collection-contract inventory supports only 4,000 input tonnes/year in the base. It anchors accessible supply, not selling price, permits or the 12,000-tonne demand assumption. No growth bridge supports the high case beyond the supplied fictional scenario.

## Break-even and evidence gate

The £150 contribution is per INPUT tonne, already net of variable costs. Required input = £1,200,000 fixed cost / £150 = 8,000 tonnes/year. Required operational utilization = 8,000/16,000 = 50% (or 40% of nameplate; do not mix denominators).

Base contribution is £600,000, leaving a £600,000 annual operating shortfall before any unprovided capital costs. Low/high shortfalls are £840,000/£300,000. Even high accessible feedstock remains below 8,000 tonnes. Recovery yield is used to report output, not multiplied into an input-tonne contribution margin.

The next gate is evidence for at least 8,000 qualified accessible input tonnes/year on a consistent contract/time basis, or a documented change to contribution/fixed costs. Commercial should validate contract delivery and feedstock quality; operations should test yield/uptime; finance should validate the contribution definition and omitted capital economics. Regulatory specialists must assess permits separately; no permission is assumed.

scores.evidence: processed input = min(accessible feedstock, operational input capacity, qualified demand in equivalent input tonnes)
scores.rationale: The output separates input supply, operational capacity, demand, yield and the utilization denominator.
Low, base and high cases use the same constraint/yield logic and retain consistent input versus output units.
The break-even calculation uses input-tonne contribution and shows why every provided supply case fails the gate.
